Appendix A Preparing initial states

In this section, we present our proposal to prepare the initial states used in the main text. Our considerations focus on the experimental accessibility and fidelity of the states created. For the FHM and the EFHM, we choose the one-particle-per-site SU(2) singlet product state as our initial state

|ψ0⟩=|singlet⟩​|singlet⟩​…​|singlet⟩,\ket{\psi_{0}}=\ket{\text{singlet}}\ket{\text{singlet}}\dots\ket{\text{singlet}}, (27)

where

|singlet⟩=12​(cL↑†​cR↓†+cR↑†​cL↓†)​|0⟩.\ket{\text{singlet}}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\left(c^{\dagger}_{L\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{R\downarrow}+c^{\dagger}_{R\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{L\downarrow}\right)\ket{0}. (28)

This is a state that can be experimentally realized with high fidelity by various methods. In our proposed experiment setup, there are two interfering laser beams with a 2:12:1 wavelength ratio. One straightforward method, demonstrated in Ref. [112], is first turning on only the long wavelength lattice, and loading two atoms into each site of the lattice (Fig. A1a). Then, one adiabatically ramps up the short-wavelength lattice such that the doublons in the original long-wavelength lattice split into a singlet across the two wells of the double-well superlattice (Fig. A1b). Alternatively, as Ref. [46] recently demonstrated, if one ramps up the short wavelength lattice with a strong magnetic gradient instead, this prepares an |↑,↓⟩\ket{\uparrow,\downarrow} state, and then one can perform a SWAP\sqrt{\mathrm{SWAP}} entangling gate followed by a quarter-cycle singlet-triplet oscillation using another magnetic field gradient, with a fidelity for the entangling gate of ∼99.75%\sim 99.75\%.

Our initial state choice is slightly different for the hardcore bosonic HHM. To get the right density for the filling ν=1/m\nu=1/m Laughlin state, we need Np=ϕ​N□2​π​mN_{p}=\frac{\phi N_{\Box}}{2\pi m} particles, where N□N_{\Box} is the number of plaquettes (i.e., the area). For ϕ=2​π/4\phi=2\pi/4, this implies Np=N□/8N_{p}=N_{\Box}/8. Therefore, we consider systems with tiled 8-site unit cells, giving Ns=Lx×Ly=(1+4​nx)×(1+2​ny)N_{s}=L_{x}\times L_{y}=(1+4n_{x})\times(1+2n_{y}) site lattices (nx,ny∈ℤn_{x},n_{y}\in\mathbb{Z}), resulting in N□=(Lx−1)×(Ly−1)=8​nx​nyN_{\Box}=(L_{x}-1)\times(L_{y}-1)=8n_{x}n_{y} plaquettes. Accordingly, we choose an initial state that is a product state with one particle localized at a single site in each 4×24\times 2 cell, as illustrated in Fig. A2. This can be prepared by selectively tuning on-site potentials at specific sites during atom loading.

Our initial state choice is different from the strategy used in many qubit-based VQE methods. In VQE methods such as the unitary coupled-cluster (UCCSD) ansatzes [48], the initial state in the ansatz to find the Hamiltonian ground state is usually the Hartree-Fock product state, which shortens the “distance” to the target state. The combination of the Hartree-Fock or other initial state preparation is an interesting direction for future study.

Appendix B Energy error scalings

Sec. V estimates the leading asymptotic scaling of the VQE error with computational time TT for critical systems and compares it with the same scaling for exact diagonalization (ED). In this Appendix, we extend that discussion in three directions. First, we refine the VQE derivation to include the first subleading contribution from the logarithmic simulation overhead in Eq. (16), which produces an algebraic prefactor for ϵ\epsilon as a function of TT. Second, we derive the corresponding leading-order scalings for gapped systems. Third, we compare the leading-order results with the scaling for matrix product state (MPS) methods for both gapped and critical systems in 1D. The resulting asymptotic scalings are summarized in Table 1.

B.1 Error scaling of critical systems for VQE

B.1.1 Refined asymptotic derivation of the VQE error scaling

The main text gives the leading-order dependence of the quantum simulation error ϵQ\epsilon_{Q} on the total evolution time TT and the system size LL. Here we derive the first subleading correction, an algebraic prefactor in T⁡(ϵQ)T(\epsilon_{Q}), arising from the HHKL’s logarithmic simulation overhead in Eq. (16).

Starting from the adiabatic bound at a system size NsN_{s} and a large τ\tau

ϵA≤CA​e−c1​(Δ​τ)1/D,\epsilon_{A}\leq C_{A}e^{-c_{1}(\Delta\tau)^{1/D}}, (29)

we obtain

τ∼1Δ​[log⁡(CA/ϵA)]D.\tau\sim\frac{1}{\Delta}\left[\log(C_{A}/\epsilon_{A})\right]^{D}. (30)

Balancing this with the quantum simulation error arising from HHKL, ϵA=ϵS\epsilon_{A}=\epsilon_{S}, gives a total error ϵQ=2​ϵA\epsilon_{Q}=2\epsilon_{A}, so rewriting log⁡(CA/ϵA)=log⁡(2​CA/ϵQ)\log(C_{A}/\epsilon_{A})=\log(2C_{A}/\epsilon_{Q}) and defining

x:=log⁡(1/ϵQ),w:=x+log⁡(2​CA)x:=\log(1/\epsilon_{Q}),\quad w:=x+\log(2C_{A}) (31)

gives

τ∼wDΔ∼1Δ​[x+log⁡(2​CA)]D.\tau\sim\frac{w^{D}}{\Delta}\sim\frac{1}{\Delta}\left[x+\log(2C_{A})\right]^{D}. (32)

Substituting τ\tau into the estimate Eq. (17), Nl∼Nsq+1​τ​log⁡(Ns​τ/ϵQ)N_{l}\sim N_{s}^{q+1}\tau\log(N_{s}\tau/\epsilon_{Q}), yields

Nl∼\displaystyle N_{l}\sim\, Nsq+1Δ​[x+log⁡(2​CA)]D​log⁡(NsΔ​ϵQ​[x+log⁡(2​CA)]D).\displaystyle\frac{N_{s}^{q+1}}{\Delta}\left[x+\log(2C_{A})\right]^{D}\log\!\left(\frac{N_{s}}{\Delta\,\epsilon_{Q}}\left[x+\log(2C_{A})\right]^{D}\right). (33)

Since T∝NlT\propto N_{l} and Ns∼LDN_{s}\sim L^{D}, Δ∼L−z\Delta\sim L^{-z} so that Nsq+1Δ∼Lb\frac{N_{s}^{q+1}}{\Delta}\sim L^{b} with b=D⁡(q+1)+zb=D(q+1)+z, we write

T∼\displaystyle T\sim\, Lb​[x+log⁡(2​CA)]D\displaystyle L^{b}\left[x+\log(2C_{A})\right]^{D}
×{x+(D+z)​log⁡L+D​log⁡[x+log⁡(2​CA)]}\displaystyle\times\left\{x+(D+z)\log\!L+D\log\!\left[x+\log(2C_{A})\right]\right\} (34)

Eq. (34) gives the relation between ϵQ\epsilon_{Q} and TT. To understand it, we expand it in the regimes of interest. For large-xx, i.e. small-ϵQ\epsilon_{Q}, the binomial expansion of Eq. (32) gives

τ∼1Δ​[xD+D​xD−1​log⁡(2​CA)+…],\tau\sim\frac{1}{\Delta}\left[x^{D}+Dx^{D-1}\log(2C_{A})+\dots\right], (35)

so Eq. (34) simplifies to

TLb∼xD​[x+D​log⁡x+(D+z)​log⁡L+B+⋯],\frac{T}{L^{b}}\sim x^{D}\left[x+D\log x+(D+z)\log\!L+B+\cdots\right], (36)

where BB is an LL-independent constant. We note that in the later theory derivation, we balance ϵQ∼ϵL\epsilon_{Q}\sim\epsilon_{L} which implies x∼p​log⁡Lx\sim\!p\log\!L. Defining

y:=(TLb)1D+1,y:=\left(\frac{T}{L^{b}}\right)^{\frac{1}{D+1}}, (37)

Eq. (34) then becomes

yD+1=cD​xD+1+D​xD​log⁡x+B​xD+⋯,y^{D+1}=c_{D}x^{D+1}+Dx^{D}\log x+Bx^{D}+\cdots, (38)

with cDc_{D} a DD-dependent constant.

To invert Eq. (38) at the large-xx limit, we use the asymptotic ansatz with the unknowns uu and vv:

x=c2​(y−u​log⁡y−v+⋯),x=c_{2}(y-u\log y-v+\cdots), (39)

and we will see that constant uu and vv suffice to asymptotically satisfy Eq. (38). Substituting this ansatz into Eq. (38), the equation is satisfied to leading order (yD+1y^{D+1} terms); solving for uu and vv to obtain the next two orders (yD​log⁡yy^{D}\log y and yDy^{D} terms) gives

x=c2​[y−D(D+1)​cD​log⁡y−B(D+1)​cD+⋯].x=c_{2}\left[y-\frac{D}{(D+1)c_{D}}\log y-\frac{B}{(D+1)c_{D}}+\cdots\right]. (40)

Substituting the definitions of xx and yy leads to the final result

ϵQ​(T,L)∼C​(TLb)γ​exp⁡[−c2​(TLb)1D+1],\epsilon_{Q}(T,L)\sim C\left(\frac{T}{L^{b}}\right)^{\gamma}\exp\left[-c_{2}\left(\frac{T}{L^{b}}\right)^{\frac{1}{D+1}}\right], (41)

where γ\gamma and CC are independent of TT and LL. This formula is the leading order result for ϵQ≪1\epsilon_{Q}\ll 1.

In addition to the x∼log⁡Lx\sim\log\!L limit, one can consider the fixed-LL limit with L≪xL\ll x, as visible at long times limit in Fig. 2, and a similar asymptotic analysis to the above leads to an extra LL-dependence in the prefactor

ϵQ​(T,L)∼C​Lβ​(TLb)γ​exp⁡[−c2​(TLb)1D+1],\epsilon_{Q}(T,L)\sim CL^{\beta}\left(\frac{T}{L^{b}}\right)^{\gamma}\exp\left[-c_{2}\left(\frac{T}{L^{b}}\right)^{\frac{1}{D+1}}\right], (42)

where β\beta is also independent of TT and LL.

B.1.2 Numerically evaluating the fixed-TT finite-size scaling of the VQE energy error

In the last subsection, we carefully derived the asymptotic VQE energy-error scaling in the T≫LbT\gg L^{b} regime, summarized by Eq. (41). In particular, at fixed LL and large TT, this scaling reduces to ϵQ∼exp⁡[−f⁡(L)​T1/(D+1)]\epsilon_{Q}\sim\exp\left[-f(L)T^{1/(D+1)}\right], which is consistent with the fixed-LL numerics shown in Fig. 2 of the main text.

However, this asymptotic expression does not apply to the VQE error ϵQ​(L,T)\epsilon_{Q}(L;T) for fixed TT when taking the thermodynamic limit. This is because the assumption T≫LbT\gg L^{b} is violated when L→∞L\to\infty for any fixed TT. We note that this limit is not necessary for obtaining the scaling advantage discussed in the main text, but is nevertheless interesting to consider.

To understand the behavior of ϵQ(L→∞;T)\epsilon_{Q}(L\to\infty;T) with TT, we obtain the L→∞L\to\infty values by numerically extrapolating the finite-LL ϵQ\epsilon_{Q} at fixed TT to L=∞L=\infty. Fig. B1 plots the ϵQ​(L,T)\epsilon_{Q}(L;T) data versus 1/L1/L. The data collapse into straight lines at the largest LL’s, which suggest that they follow a finite-size scaling

ϵQ​(L,T)=ϵQ​(∞,T)+A⁡(T)L.\epsilon_{Q}(L;T)=\epsilon_{Q}(\infty;T)+\frac{A(T)}{L}. (43)

The parameters ϵQ​(∞,T)\epsilon_{Q}(\infty;T) and A⁡(T)A(T) can then be extracted by the linear fits of data points of the largest LL’s. At each fixed TT, the VQE error approaches a finite intercept ϵQ​(∞,T)\epsilon_{Q}(\infty;T) as 1/L→01/L\to 0, which decreases as TT increases – the error remains finite in the L→∞L\to\infty limit and increasing TT reduces the VQE error, even in the thermodynamic limit.

B.2 Error scaling of gapped systems for ED and VQE

We have shown the error scaling of ED and VQE for critical systems in Sec. V. The same analysis from Eq. (13) to Eq. (23) can be readily extended to the gapped systems, with the replacement of the finite-size error ϵL∼L−p\epsilon_{L}\sim L^{-p} with ∼e−L/L0\sim e^{-L/L_{0}} [93], where L0L_{0} is the correlation length. Applying this change and that L∼log1/D⁡TL\sim\log^{1/D}T for ED, the ED error is

ϵ∼e−L/L0∼exp[−log1/D⁡TL0].\epsilon\sim e^{-L/L_{0}}\sim\exp\left[-\frac{\log^{1/D}T}{L_{0}}\right]. (44)

For VQE, since the finite-size error is changed and the gap is present, the quantum simulation error ϵQ\epsilon_{Q} can be derived from Eq. (34) by assuming x∼L≫1x\sim L\gg 1. This yields the same result, Eq. (20), with z=0z=0 and minor modifications to the prefactor. The optimal size L⁡(T∗)L(T^{*}) to satisfy Eq. (21) becomes

L⁡(T∗)∼(Δ​T∗​L0D+1)1D​q+2​D+1,L(T^{*})\sim(\Delta T^{*}L^{D+1}_{0})^{\frac{1}{Dq+2D+1}}, (45)

and the algorithm error for VQE when choosing the optimal LL for a time T∗T^{*} is

ϵ=ϵQ+ϵL∼exp⁡[−(Δ​T∗L0D⁡(q+1))1D​q+2​D+1].\epsilon=\epsilon_{Q}+\epsilon_{L}\sim\exp\left[-\left(\frac{\Delta T^{*}}{L_{0}^{D(q+1)}}\right)^{\frac{1}{Dq+2D+1}}\right]. (46)

Compared to the ED error scaling Eq. (44), this is also an exponential improvement in the runtime required to reach fixed error, similar to the quantum improvement in the case of critical systems shown in the main text.

B.3 Error scaling for 1D MPS

In this subsection, we compare the fVQE error convergence with that of MPS algorithms by deriving how the finite-size and bond-dimension errors scale with computational time for the models considered in the main text. MPS is a variational ansatz that has errors from both its finite size ϵL\epsilon_{L} and its finite bond dimensions ϵE\epsilon_{E}, i.e., the finite entanglement it captures by a truncated maximal bond dimension χ\chi. The finite-size error ϵL\epsilon_{L} of MPS scales identically to that of ED and VQE. The finite-bond error ϵE\epsilon_{E} has also been studied by past literature for 1D critical systems [94, 95], and a rigorous upper bound of ϵE\epsilon_{E} has also been shown for 1D gapped systems [113, 114]. We translate these results into our framework for both critical and gapped systems.

B.3.1 Critical system

The FHM and EFHM in this work have gapless ground states in the thermodynamic limit, described by a conformal field theory (CFT) with central charge c=1c=1. The HHM is gapped in the bulk, but hosts a gapless c=1c=1 CFT on the boundary. For these models, ϵL∼L−p\epsilon_{L}\sim L^{-p}, and we estimate p=1p=1 from numerical extrapolation. On the other hand, for infinite system size, L→∞L\to\infty, the finite bond dimension χ\chi for a theory with central charge cc gives an error for local observable [94, 95]

ϵE∼1ξa∼1χa​κ,\epsilon_{E}\sim\frac{1}{\xi^{a}}\sim\frac{1}{\chi^{a\kappa}}, (47)

where aa is an observable-dependent constant and a=2a=2 for energy density, the large but finite correlation length ξ∼χκ\xi\sim\chi^{\kappa} is the effective correlation length that the finite bond dimension MPS can capture, and the exponent is

κ=6c⁡(12/c+1),\kappa=\frac{6}{c\left(\sqrt{12/c}+1\right)}, (48)

To achieve a desired total error, both finite-size error and finite-entanglement error must be controlled, i.e. sufficiently large LL and χ\chi must be taken simultaneously. To minimize the asymptotic total error ϵ=ϵL+ϵE\epsilon=\epsilon_{L}+\epsilon_{E} for a given computational time, which scales as T∼L​χ3T\sim L\chi^{3} for each MPS sweep, one should take the optimal χ∗∼Lp/(a​κ)\chi^{*}\sim L^{p/(a\kappa)} to balance ϵL=ϵE\epsilon_{L}=\epsilon_{E}. This choice also gives ξ∝Lp/a≪L\xi\propto L^{p/a}\ll L, self-consistently ensuring that Eq. (47) is valid at the chosen χ∗\chi^{*}. Then the total error depends on the run-time as

ϵ=ϵL+ϵE∼T−p1+3​p/(a​κ).\epsilon=\epsilon_{L}+\epsilon_{E}\sim T^{-\frac{p}{1+3p/(a\kappa)}}. (49)

For p=c=1p=c=1, a=2a=2, the exponent is about 0.470.47.

The power law scaling holds for space complexity as well, as the spatial resources scale as M∼L​χ2∼L1+2​p/(a​κ)M\sim L\chi^{2}\sim L^{1+2p/(a\kappa)}, resulting in the MPS energy error decay with classical memory

ϵ∼M−p1+p/κ.\epsilon\sim M^{-\frac{p}{1+p/\kappa}}. (50)

Fig. B2 displays the same data as Fig. 2 of the main text, now with the MPS error scaling versus time. Only the slopes on the log-log plots are meaningful for comparison, as the prefactors are arbitrary and set for visual convenience. Remarkably, even in these one-dimensional cases where MPS is expected to be efficient, the VQE matches or exceeds the convergence rate of MPS. This strongly suggests that the VQE will have an even larger advantage in higher dimensions, where we expect the VQE scaling to be similar, while the MPS complexity will scale exponentially with the width of the system.

B.3.2 Gapped system

Finally, we briefly discuss the MPS error scaling of the gapped systems. We note that the bound quoted here is a rigorous upper bound on local-approximation error as a function of bond dimension, and is generally considerably more pessimistic than what is observed in DMRG calculations on simple gapped chains.

According to Refs. [115, 114], the finite bond-dimension error ϵE\epsilon_{E} of approximating the exact ground state of an LL-site 1D gapped local Hamiltonian is upper bounded by the maximal bond dimension χ\chi as

ϵE≤CE​L​e−cχ​log4/3​χ,\epsilon_{E}\leq C_{E}Le^{-c_{\chi}\log^{4/3}{\chi}}, (51)

with CEC_{E} and cχc_{\chi} LL-independent constants. As the finite-size error ϵL\epsilon_{L} scales identically as in the ED case, to minimize the asymptotic total error ϵL+ϵE\epsilon_{L}+\epsilon_{E} when LL approaches the thermodynamic limit, we increase the bond dimension χ∗\chi^{*} simultaneously with LL so that ϵE​(χ∗)=ϵL​(L)\epsilon_{E}(\chi^{*})=\epsilon_{L}(L). At large LL, such an optimal increase of χ∗\chi^{*} is asymptotically given by

χ∗∼ecχ′​L3/4,\chi^{*}\sim e^{c^{\prime}_{\chi}L^{3/4}}, (52)

with constant cχ′c^{\prime}_{\chi}. With the time complexity T∼L​χ3T\sim L\chi^{3}, we obtain the MPS error scaling for the gapped 1D chain

ϵ∼exp⁡[−cM​log4/3​T].\epsilon\sim\exp\left[-c_{M}\log^{4/3}T\right]. (53)

This is a decay faster than any power law.

From the above discussions, we find that the MPS methods are comparably efficient with VQE for 1D and quasi-1D systems (a power law speedup for fVQE, if any). However, as we pointed out in Sec. V, if one uses a 1D MPS representation for a higher-dimensional lattice, the required bond dimension grows exponentially with the transverse width, resulting in an overall computational complexity that is significantly higher than that of the fVQE method.

Appendix C Optimization method

This section details the optimization method we use. We perform a standard SLSQP optimization algorithm where each parameter is constrained to an interval as described in App. C.1, and we iterate the algorithm until consecutive cost function values agree within 10−610^{-6}.

The variational parameters used in the optimization algorithm are dimensionless. For the FHM and EFHM the parameters are t1,2(m)/U~0t^{(m)}_{1,2}/\tilde{U}_{0}, μF,1(m)/U~0\mu^{(m)}_{F,1}/\tilde{U}_{0}, μF,2(m)/U~0\mu^{(m)}_{F,2}/\tilde{U}_{0}, and T(m)​U~0T^{(m)}\tilde{U}_{0}. For the HHM, since U~0→∞\tilde{U}_{0}\to\infty, we instead use the dimensionless parameters tx​1(m)​T(m),tx​2(m)​T(m),ty(m)​T(m),μQ(m)​T(m)t_{x1}^{(m)}T^{(m)},\,t_{x2}^{(m)}T^{(m)},\,t_{y}^{(m)}T^{(m)},\,\mu_{Q}^{(m)}T^{(m)} and μS(m)​T(m)\mu_{S}^{(m)}T^{(m)} .

To efficiently seed the SLSQP initial values, we use what we call “bootstrap” and “transfer” techniques that optimize large NlN_{l} and LL ansatzes using information obtained from smaller NlN_{l} and LL solutions. To do this, for each data point in Fig. 2, we perform 101101 runs – in three classes described momentarily – and choose the best result. 5050 of the runs start from random initial parameter guesses sampled from a uniform distribution in the allowed windows that will be given in Table 2 and 3 of App. C.1. Another 5050 runs start from initial guesses using the bootstrap technique described in App. C.2, which uses results from Nl−1N_{l}-1 layers (if any exist) to seed the NlN_{l}-layer calculation. A final run uses the transfer technique described in App. C.3, which uses results from L−2L-2 (if they exist) to seed the LL-site calculation. The calculation starts from Nl=1N_{l}=1 and small LL (usually around L=4L=4) and iteratively increases NlN_{l} to the maximum value considered, then increments LL and repeats. For the largest LL (L=13L=13 and 1414 for the FHM and L=14L=14 for the EFHM), doing 101101 runs for each case became too expensive, so we used a single run based on the transfer technique, which was found to work well.

Despite its simplicity, this optimization procedure is efficient enough to be useful, with the number of iterations NiterN_{\text{iter}} growing slowly with the system size LL and (roughly linearly) with the number of layers NlN_{l}. Although improving the optimization cost for the VQE is not a major focus of this work, these results suggest that the ansatz may be optimized efficiently even for much larger systems, in particular in the sense that the optimization costs do not eliminate the exponential scaling advantage of runtime. There are many routes to improved optimization, which are left for future work.

C.1 Parameter windows

Our variational parameter space is restricted by experimental concerns and to enhance the efficiency and analysis of scaling of our optimization. Experimental concerns such as avoiding band mixing and rapid parameter changes constrain the parameters. Some such constraints – for instance, fixing the large Hubbard interaction at U(m)=U~0U^{(m)}=\tilde{U}_{0} – have been reflected in our ansatz. The experimental capabilities restrict the tunneling and on-site potential to be not much larger than UU. Also, the signs of all tunnelings tt’s need to be positive. So we limit 0≤t/U~0≤10\leq t/\tilde{U}_{0}\leq 1 and |μ/U~0|≤1|\mu/\tilde{U}_{0}|\leq 1. To avoid the uncontrolled growth of ansatz evolution time, we limit the time parameter 0≤T(m)​U~0≤π0\leq T^{(m)}\tilde{U}_{0}\leq\pi.

Second, limiting parameter windows enhances the efficiency of the optimization algorithm. While a larger parameter window may contain better local minima on the variational energy landscape, searching this larger space is significantly slower and may contain many local minima and barren plateaus. To find the most efficient parameter windows, we started with the broadest ranges allowed by experimental restrictions and then systematically tested progressively narrower windows. For FHM and EFHM, we performed these tests on small systems with L=6L=6 (L=5L=5 for odd LL). Specifically, we tested the windows of the drive Hamiltonian parameters t/U~0t/\tilde{U}_{0}’s and |μ/U~0||\mu/\tilde{U}_{0}| progressively from [0,1][0,1] to [0,0.5][0,0.5] and [0,0.25][0,0.25]. The optimal windows are shown in Table 2.

For the HHM with parameters μQ(m)​T(m)\mu_{Q}^{(m)}T^{(m)} and μS(m)​T(m)\mu_{S}^{(m)}T^{(m)}, we compare between [−π,π][-\pi,\pi] and [−0.5​π,0.5​π][-0.5\pi,0.5\pi]. The optimal parameter window is shown in Table 3.

C.2 Bootstrap technique

To optimize large NlN_{l} ansatzes efficiently, we use the bootstrap technique to generate good initial guesses given results from smaller NlN_{l} ansatzes. For a number of layers NlN_{l}, we use an initial guess where the first Nl−1N_{l}-1 layers use the solution for the Nl−1N_{l}-1-layer problem, and the last layer’s parameters are chosen randomly. As shown in Figs. C1a– c for the L=12L=12 FHM, the ansatz parameters converge to a smooth function of the layer index mm, as the total number of layers NlN_{l} increases. This convergence suggests the applicability of the bootstrap scheme – effectively, it implies that parameters in the earlier layers need only minor adjustments when a new layer is added.

C.3 Transfer technique

In addition to the fully random initial guesses and the bootstrap (using random initial guesses for the last layer), we also use the transfer technique to optimize ansatzes of large LL lattices using smaller LL results without extra random guesses. This is particularly straightforward since our ansatzes use LL-independent parameterizations. Additionally, we expect the parameters to depend weakly on LL for large LL. (This is suggested by finite-size scaling bounding how the true result varies and Lieb-Robinson arguments applied to the VQE dynamics.) This suggests the transfer procedure: we run one optimization of size-LL NlN_{l}-layer VQE, using the optimal L−2L-2 NlN_{l}-layer VQE result as the initial guess. The number of optimization steps following this guess grows more slowly with LL and NlN_{l} than for fully random guesses. Figs. C1d–f show that the parameters in the Nl=10N_{l}=10 ansatz for the even-LL FHM converge to smooth function of mm at large LL, analogous to the convergence found for our bootstrap technique with large NlN_{l}. This shows the utility of the transfer technique.

C.4 Iteration number scaling

Finally, Fig. C2 shows the growth of the iteration numbers needed to reach convergence for each ansatz depth NlN_{l} and size LL for all models in Fig. 2. The total number of iterations NiterN_{\text{iter}} does not grow significantly with LL, perhaps even decreasing, and increases slowly (very roughly at most linearly) with NlN_{l}. Notably, NiterN_{\text{iter}} for the largest LL runs using only the transfer technique is less than the iterations used to optimize at smaller LL. As the total quantum algorithm run-time has to be multiplied by a factor NiterN_{\text{iter}} as Niter​TN_{\text{iter}}T, the slow growth of NiterN_{\text{iter}} with both LL and NlN_{l} suggests that the exponential quantum speedup we claim in the main text based on the scaling of TT can survive even after accounting for the many shots needed for optimization.

Appendix D Total quantum evolution time

A key consideration in this work is the numerical scaling of the VQE algorithm error as a function of the total quantum evolution time TT, the sum of the time parameters over all ansatz layers:

T=∑mT(m).T=\sum_{m}T^{(m)}. (54)

However, the time parameters T(m)T^{(m)} have a physical unit of time, which makes their absolute values depend on the physical setup; in contrast, the optimization parameters in the VQE algorithm are dimensionless, e.g. tx​1(m)​T(m)t_{x1}^{(m)}T^{(m)}. To relate the total quantum evolution time TT to the dimensionless variational parameters, it is helpful to convert TT to a dimensionless parameter independent of the actual experimental time scale. This section addresses this for the FHM, EFHM, and HHM.

As mentioned in Sec. II, for the FHM and EFHM, we take U(m)=U~0U^{(m)}=\tilde{U}_{0} to be fixed at each layer for simplicity. (This is also the frequency unit, since we set ℏ=1\hbar=1). It is straightforward to make TT dimensionless by multiplying U~0\tilde{U}_{0} on both sides of Eq. (54):

T​U~0=∑mT(m)​U~0.T\tilde{U}_{0}=\sum_{m}T^{(m)}\tilde{U}_{0}. (55)

This means the dimensionless total time T​U~0T\tilde{U}_{0} is also the sum of dimensionless variational parameters T(m)​U~0T^{(m)}\tilde{U}_{0} used in the numerical optimization.

For the hardcore HHM, U(m)→∞U^{(m)}\to\infty is no longer a useful reference energy. Thus we need to find another fixed frequency scale f~0\tilde{f}_{0} to make TT dimensionless. As an aside, we note this is necessary only for characterizing the total optimization time, not for performing the numerical optimization, which can work directly with the dimensionless variational parameters θx​1=tx​1(m)​T(m),θx​2=tx​2(m)​T(m),θy=ty(m)​T(m)\theta_{x1}=t_{x1}^{(m)}T^{(m)},\,\theta_{x2}=t_{x2}^{(m)}T^{(m)},\,\theta_{y}=t_{y}^{(m)}T^{(m)}, θQ=μQ(m)​T(m)\theta_{Q}=\mu_{Q}^{(m)}T^{(m)} and θS=μS(m)​T(m)\theta_{S}=\mu_{S}^{(m)}T^{(m)}. To determine T=∑mT(m)T=\sum_{m}T^{(m)} from the dimensionless variational parameters, we define

T(m)=max⁡{θx​1t~max,θx​2t~max,θyt~max,|θQ|Q​t~max,|θS|Q​t~max}T^{(m)}=\max\left\{\frac{\theta_{x1}}{\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}}},\,\frac{\theta_{x2}}{\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}}},\,\frac{\theta_{y}}{\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}}},\,\frac{|\theta_{Q}|}{Q\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}}},\,\frac{|\theta_{S}|}{Q\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}}}\right\} (56)

where t~max{\tilde{t}}_{\text{max}} is the maximum tunneling rate that can be applied experimentally, and Q​t~maxQ{\tilde{t}}_{\text{max}} with Q>1Q>1 is the maximum on-site potential that can be applied experimentally. This choice of T(m)T^{(m)} characterizes the total time relative to T​t~maxT\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}} if one maximizes the tunnelings and on-site potential consistent with these constraints, thus giving the shortest time evolution consistent with the numerically chosen dimensionless optimization parameters. In this work, we choose Q=3/2Q=3/2.

Summing over all ansatz layers, we relate the dimensionless total evolution time TT to the dimensionless variational parameters by

T​t~max=∑mmax⁡{θx​1,θx​2,θy,|θQ|Q,|θS|Q}.T\tilde{t}_{\mathrm{max}}=\sum_{m}\max\left\{\theta_{x1},\,\theta_{x2},\,\theta_{y},\,\frac{|\theta_{Q}|}{Q},\,\frac{|\theta_{S}|}{Q}\right\}. (57)

Appendix E Universal gate set

In this section, we demonstrate that the native Hamiltonians in our framework can implement a universal set of fermionic operations. Universal fermionic quantum gate sets have been constructed using local fermionic (but number non-conserving) operations [45] and also from particle-number-conserving operations [82, 116]. Specifically, from the theory of simple Lie algebra, Ref. [82] proves that a fermionic quantum gate set generates the full 𝔰​𝔲​(ℋ)\mathfrak{su}(\mathcal{H}) algebra in any NpN_{p}-particle subspace ℋ\mathcal{H} of the MM fermion modes Fock space if it includes two ingredients: (1) arbitrary evolutions generated by two-mode tunneling Hamiltonians:

Ga​btun​(𝜽)\displaystyle G^{\mathrm{tun}}_{ab}(\bm{\theta}) =\displaystyle= exp{−i\displaystyle\!\!\!\exp\Big\{\!-i\, [θ12(e−i​θ2ca†cb+h.c.)\displaystyle\Big[\frac{\theta_{1}}{2}\left(e^{-i\theta_{2}}c_{a}^{\dagger}c_{b}+\mathrm{h.c.}\right)
+θ32(na−nb)]}∀a,b∈ℐM,\displaystyle\hskip 0.0pt{}+\frac{\theta_{3}}{2}\left(n_{a}-n_{b}\right)\Big]\Big\}\hskip 10.84006pt\forall a,b\in\mathcal{I}_{M}, (58)

and (2) any two-mode non-quadratic “interaction” gate

Gc​dint​(θ)=exp⁡{−i​θ​nc​nd}G^{\mathrm{int}}_{cd}(\theta)=\exp\left\{-i\theta n_{c}n_{d}\right\} (59)

for some cc and d∈ℐMd\in\mathcal{I}_{M}, where ℐM={(1,↑),(1,↓),…,(Ns,↓)}\mathcal{I}_{M}=\{(1,\uparrow),(1,\downarrow),\dots,(N_{s},\downarrow)\} is the set of fermion mode indices. Here and in the rest of the section, unless explicitly specified, we use a,b,…a,b,\dots to refer to lumped site and spin indices (i,σ)(i,\sigma) (with the spin index taking two values for the FHM and EFHM, and a single value for the HHM).

Therefore, to show our fVQE framework’s universality in any particle-number-conserving sector, we show that the Hamiltonian Eq. (1) augmented with local spin-dependent terms,

HSR(m)=H(m)+∑i𝑩i(m)⋅𝑺i,H^{(m)}_{\mathrm{SR}}=H^{(m)}+\sum_{i}\bm{B}^{(m)}_{i}\cdot\bm{S}_{i}, (60)

can be used to engineer arbitrary Ga​btunG^{\mathrm{tun}}_{ab} and one Gc​dintG^{\mathrm{int}}_{cd}. We note that the spin-dependent terms involving fermionic spin-1/21/2 operators 𝑺i=(Six,Siy,Siz)\bm{S}_{i}=(S^{x}_{i},S^{y}_{i},S^{z}_{i}) with tunable magnetic field parameters 𝑩i=(Bix,Biy,Biz)\bm{B}_{i}=(B^{x}_{i},B^{y}_{i},B^{z}_{i}) are not used for the protocols in the main text, a point we discuss further at the end of this subsection. The single-spin rotations can be engineered as follows: local SzS^{z} rotations can be implemented by a single-site resolved laser with a vector light shift [117, 118] that couples the two (pseudo-)spin levels |↑⟩\ket{\uparrow}, |↓⟩\ket{\downarrow}, and local SxS^{x}, SyS^{y} rotations can be realized by Raman coupling between the two spin levels with a focused laser. For simplicity in the rest of this section, we suppress the circuit layer index (m)(m), and we use t1t_{1} and t2t_{2} to denote the strong (intra-cell) and weak (inter-cell) tunnelings in the optical superlattice. We also use μi,σ\mu_{i,\sigma} to denote a mode-specific potential μi,σ=μi+σ​Biz2\mu_{i,\sigma}=\mu_{i}+\sigma\frac{B^{z}_{i}}{2}, using σ=+1\sigma=+1 and −1-1 and ↑\uparrow and ↓\downarrow interchangeably.

The uniform Hubbard interaction U​ni,↑​ni,↓Un_{i,\uparrow}n_{i,\downarrow} gives the required interaction gate Gc​dintG^{\mathrm{int}}_{cd} [82]. It then remains to show we can generate arbitrary two-mode tunnelings Eq. (58).

Ga​btun=Rb​cx(π/2)Ga​ctunRc​bx(−π/2)\displaystyle G^{\mathrm{tun}}_{ab}=R^{x}_{bc}(\pi/2)\,G^{\mathrm{tun}}_{ac}\,R^{x}_{cb}(-\pi/2) (63)

where Ga​ctunG^{\mathrm{tun}}_{ac} now acts on nearest neighbors, and ↑\uparrow and ↓\downarrow are considered “nearest-neighbors” along an artificial extra dimension. Now we turn to the only missing piece in the above construction, the neighboring-site tunneling gate Ra​bxR^{x}_{ab}. We show how to synthesize this gate, without loss of generality, on bond (1,↑)↔(2,↑)(1,\uparrow)\leftrightarrow(2,\uparrow) using the drive Hamiltonian Eq. (60). The idea is to suppress the tunneling on all bonds not involved in the tunneling by applying a strong staggered on-site potential μi,σ\mu_{i,\sigma} across them; on the target bond, we keep the coherent tunneling by tuning each pair of tunnel-coupled sites to resonance. We now present this idea in detail.

We start from Eq. (60):

Utun≡exp⁡[−i​T​HSR​(t1=θ/T,t2=0,μi,σ)]U^{\mathrm{tun}}\equiv\exp\left[-iTH_{\mathrm{SR}}(t_{1}=\theta/T,t_{2}=0,\mu_{i,\sigma})\right] (64)

with a vanishing inter-cell tunneling t2=0t_{2}=0 to isolate each double-well from the others.

After this tunneling operation, we switch to applying a “phase-reverse” gate with a tunneling-free Hamiltonian:

UPR≡\displaystyle U^{\mathrm{PR}}\equiv\, exp[−iT′HSR(t1=t2=0,μi,σ′)]\displaystyle\exp\left[-iT^{\prime}H_{\mathrm{SR}}(t_{1}=t_{2}=0,\mu^{\prime}_{i,\sigma})\right]
=\displaystyle=\, exp⁡[−i​T′​(U​∑ini,↑​ni,↓−∑i,σμi,σ′​ni,σ)],\displaystyle\exp\left[-iT^{\prime}\left(U\sum_{i}n_{i,\uparrow}n_{i,\downarrow}-\sum_{i,\sigma}\mu^{\prime}_{i,\sigma}n_{i,\sigma}\right)\right], (65)

where T′=2​n​π/U−TT^{\prime}=2n\pi/U-T with the integer nn such that T′>0T^{\prime}>0, and μ′i,σ=−μi,σT/T′\mu^{\prime}_{i,\sigma}=-\mu_{i,\sigma}T/T^{\prime}.

The combination of Eq. (64) and Eq. (65), with the appropriate parameters μi,σ\mu_{i,\sigma}, suppresses all unwanted tunneling except the target one with up spin on the (1,2)(1,2) pair. We first analyze how the strong staggered potential suppresses tunneling, and then analyze how the target tunneling is energetically allowed. These will show that UPR​UtunU^{\text{PR}}U^{\text{tun}} repeated with three sets of offsets on the target sites realizes the desired R(1↑)​(2↑)x​(θ)R^{x}_{(1\uparrow)(2\uparrow)}(\theta) gate.

The derivation is based on standard time-dependent perturbation theory. If |i⟩\ket{i} is a Fock basis state, HSRH_{\mathrm{SR}} can be separated into its diagonal term HdH_{d} and off-diagonal tunneling term HtH_{t}

⟨i|​Hd​|j⟩=di​δi​j,⟨i|​Ht​|j⟩=Vi​j​(1−δi​j).\bra{i}H_{d}\ket{j}=d_{i}\delta_{ij},\quad\bra{i}H_{t}\ket{j}=V_{ij}(1-\delta_{ij}). (66)

In the interaction picture:

⟨i|​(Ht)I​(τ)​|j⟩=⟨i|​ei​Hd​τ​Ht​e−i​Hd​τ​|j⟩=Vi​j​ei​Δi​j​τ,\bra{i}(H_{t})_{I}(\tau)\ket{j}=\bra{i}e^{iH_{d}\tau}H_{t}e^{-iH_{d}\tau}\ket{j}=V_{ij}e^{i\Delta_{ij}\tau}, (67)

where Δi​j=di−dj\Delta_{ij}=d_{i}-d_{j}. Importantly, with our carefully chosen μi,σ′\mu_{i,\sigma}^{\prime} and T′T^{\prime},

UPR=e−i​T′​HSR′=ei​T​Hd,U^{\mathrm{PR}}=e^{-iT^{\prime}H^{\prime}_{\mathrm{SR}}}=e^{iTH_{d}}, (68)

effectively transforms the time evolution UtunU^{\mathrm{tun}} into the interaction picture:

UPRUtun=(Utun)I=exp[−i∫0Tdτ(Ht)I(τ)].U^{\mathrm{PR}}U^{\mathrm{tun}}=\left(U^{\mathrm{tun}}\right)_{I}=\exp\left[-i\int^{T}_{0}d\tau(H_{t})_{I}(\tau)\right]. (69)

For strong staggered potential, |Δi​j|≫Vi​j|\Delta_{ij}|\gg V_{ij}, the fast-oscillating (Ht)I(H_{t})_{I} averages out at the time scale T∼1/Vi​jT\sim 1/V_{ij}. A detailed expansion, such as the Dyson series, finds the error of dropping (Ht)I(H_{t})_{I} is O⁡(Vi​j/Δi​j)O(V_{ij}/\Delta_{ij}).

We can analyze each double well individually, since the Hamiltonians that generate the time evolution commute between different double wells. We begin by considering a double-well (a,b)(a,b), and the general tunneling term in the interaction picture is

(Ht)I(τ)=−t1∑σei⁡(U​Δ​na​b,σ¯−Δ​μa​b,σ)​τca,σ†cb,σ+h.c.,(H_{t})_{I}(\tau)=-t_{1}\sum_{\sigma}e^{i(U\Delta n_{ab,{\bar{\sigma}}}-\Delta\mu_{ab,\sigma})\tau}c^{\dagger}_{a,\sigma}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{b,\sigma}+\text{h.c.}, (70)

where σ¯\bar{\sigma} is the complement of σ\sigma, i.e. σ¯=↑\bar{\sigma}=\uparrow if σ=↓\sigma=\downarrow and σ¯=↓\bar{\sigma}=\downarrow if σ=↑\sigma=\uparrow; Δ​na​b,σ=na,σ−nb,σ\Delta n_{ab,\sigma}=n_{a,\sigma}-n_{b,\sigma}; and Δ​μa​b,σ=μa,σ−μb,σ\Delta\mu_{ab,\sigma}=\mu_{a,\sigma}-\mu_{b,\sigma}.

If (a,b)(a,b) is the unwanted cell with a,b>2a,b>2, effective tunneling terms are suppressed by a fast-oscillating phase for all Δ​na​b,σ′=0,±1\Delta n_{ab,\sigma^{\prime}}=0,\pm 1 cases with both σ=↑\sigma=\uparrow and ↓\downarrow. This is achieved by setting |Δ​μa​b|≫t1|\Delta\mu_{ab}|\gg t_{1}, |U+Δ​μa​b|≫t1|U+\Delta\mu_{ab}|\gg t_{1} and |U−Δ​μa​b|≫t1|U-\Delta\mu_{ab}|\gg t_{1}.

If (a,b)=(1,2)(a,b)=(1,2) is the target cell, we want to suppress all tunneling terms but the c1,↑†​c2,↑+h.c.c^{\dagger}_{1,\uparrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{2,\uparrow}+\rm h.c. one. To suppress spin-down tunneling, we keep Δ​μ12,↓≫t1\Delta\mu_{12,\downarrow}\gg t_{1}, as in the unwanted cells. Δ​μ12,↓\Delta\mu_{12,\downarrow} can take a wide range of values as long as |U​Δ​n12,↑−Δ​μ12,↓|≫t1|U\Delta n_{12,\uparrow}-\Delta\mu_{12,\downarrow}|\gg t_{1}; for concreteness, we set Δ​μ12,↓=U/2\Delta\mu_{12,\downarrow}=U/2.

Finally, we consider the desired resonant tunneling terms. The value of Δ​n12,↑\Delta n_{12,\uparrow} to achieve resonant tunneling depends on the densities via

Δ​μ12,↑=U​Δ​n12,↓,\Delta\mu_{12,\uparrow}=U\Delta n_{12,\downarrow}, (71)

where Δ​μ12,↓\Delta\mu_{12,\downarrow} can take values 00 and ±1\pm 1. To complete the full target tunneling gate, we propose a three-step scheme, each step of which executes the pure tunneling process for one value of the Δ​μ12,↓\Delta\mu_{12,\downarrow} while leaving the other sectors unaffected:

Rx(1,↑)(2,↑)=\displaystyle R^{x}_{(1,\uparrow)(2,\uparrow)}=\, UPR​Utun|Δ​μ12,↑=−U\displaystyle U^{\mathrm{PR}}U^{\mathrm{tun}}|_{\Delta\mu_{12,\uparrow}=-U}
×UPR​Utun|Δ​μ12,↑=U\displaystyle\hskip-10.11775pt\times U^{\mathrm{PR}}U^{\mathrm{tun}}|_{\Delta\mu_{12,\uparrow}=U}
×UPR​Utun|Δ​μ12,↑=0.\displaystyle\hskip-10.11775pt\times U^{\mathrm{PR}}U^{\mathrm{tun}}|_{\Delta\mu_{12,\uparrow}=0}. (72)

Each step can be analyzed by Eq. (69). This provides the last operation necessary to realize the arbitrary two-mode tunneling gate Ga​btunG^{\mathrm{tun}}_{ab}.

E.2 Discussions

We note that the derivation in this section differs from the previous literature, as we never assume we have local controllability over UU, nor do we need to tune to exactly U=0U=0. While our framework demonstrates universality with the assistance of local on-site potential control, an alternative is provided by the recent finding on global controllability [116] which eliminates the need for such local control but increases the cost to O⁡(Ns2)O(N^{2}_{s}) global controls, where NsN_{s} is the number of sites.

The construction shown here requires an additional ingredient compared to the drive Hamiltonian in the main text, the local spin operators. These are necessary to obtain universality. While this control is experimentally realizable as described earlier, we exclude it from our S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric fVQE ansatzes, because the dynamics and target Hamiltonians in the examples demonstrated in the main text are all S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric, and empirically the calculated fVQE energy errors converge to zero within machine precision without such terms. The rigorous proof of the universality of S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric gates into any S​U​(2)SU(2)-symmetric state space is beyond the scope of this paper (it will be given in future work).

Appendix F Correlation measurement

In this section, we discuss the experimentally accessible range of observables in our framework, which is important for two reasons. First, this tells us which properties of the ground state wavefunction we will have access to. Second, as discussed in Sec. II, to simulate a Hamiltonian HTH_{T} by the fVQE method one must obtain ⟨HT⟩\braket{H_{T}}, which can be done by measuring subsets of Hamiltonian terms and adding them together as necessary. In other words, the Hamiltonians that can be simulated are those that are sums of terms that can be experimentally measured. We now briefly discuss several important types of correlations – both for their interest in characterizing the ground states in the main text and as potential terms in the target Hamiltonian – and how they can be measured using the current experiment techniques.

F.1 Densities & two-point correlations

Site- and spin-resolved densities ⟨ni,σ⟩\braket{n_{i,\sigma}} and their correlations ⟨ni,σ​nj,τ⟩\braket{n_{i,\sigma}n_{j,\tau}} can be directly measured by quantum gas microscopy, as can general density-related moments ⟨ni,σ​nj,τ​…⟩\braket{n_{i,\sigma}n_{j,\tau}\dots}. This spin-dependent density measurement is the fundamental ingredient for all measurements we consider.

A crucial observable beyond local densities ⟨ni,σ⟩=⟨ci,σ†​ci,σ⟩\braket{n_{i,\sigma}}=\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}c_{i,\sigma}^{\phantom{\dagger}}} is off-diagonal coherence ⟨ci,σ†​cj,σ⟩\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}}, such as the tunneling terms in the kinetic energy, possibly including a gauge field. These can be measured by isolating the two wells ii and jj, performing the double-well rotation R(i,σ)​(j,σ)a​(π/2)R^{a}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(\pi/2) – one set of measurements with a=xa=x and another with a=ya=y – introduced in the prior subsection (this takes just a few time evolutions under the system Hamiltonian with appropriate double-well offsets), and then measuring the populations of each site. We are primarily interested in nearest-neighbor ii and jj, but longer-range coherences also can be measured by bringing ii and jj to neighbors using the swap techniques of App. E.1, or re-arrangement if one is using optical tweezers.

Specifically, using the operator notation X(i,σ)​(j,σ)X_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}, Y(i,σ)​(j,σ)Y_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}, and Z(i,σ)​(j,σ)Z_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)} defined in Eq. (61), we rewrite

ci,σ†​cj,σ=X(i,σ)​(j,σ)+i​Y(i,σ)​(j,σ)2.c^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}c^{{\phantom{\dagger}}}_{j,\sigma}=\frac{X_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}+iY_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}}{2}. (73)

Then

Y(i,σ)​(j,σ)=−R(i,σ)​(j,σ)x(π/2)Z(i,σ)​(j,σ)R(i,σ)​(j,σ)x(−π/2),Y_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}=-R^{x}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(\pi/2)Z_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}R^{x}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(-\pi/2), (74)

and

X(i,σ)​(j,σ)=R(i,σ)​(j,σ)y(π/2)Z(i,σ)​(j,σ)R(i,σ)​(j,σ)y(−π/2).\displaystyle X_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}=R^{y}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(\pi/2)Z_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}R^{y}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(-\pi/2). (75)

So the average populations after rotation, (1/2)​(1+⟨Z(i,σ)​(j,σ)⟩)(1/2)(1+\braket{Z_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}}), allow one to determine Z(i,σ)​(j,σ)Z_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)} and therefore the expectation values needed to obtain the coherence ⟨ci,σ†​cj,σ⟩\braket{c_{i,\sigma}^{\dagger}c_{j,\sigma}^{\phantom{\dagger}}} from Eq. (73).

In addition to the spin-invariant measurement introduced above, spin-flip two-point correlations can be measured via spin swaps.

F.2 Pairing & four-point correlations

In addition to the two-point measurements, off-diagonal two-body four-point correlations, such as the singlet pairing correlations

⟨ΔS,i†​ΔS,i+r⟩=\displaystyle\braket{\Delta^{\dagger}_{S,i}\Delta_{S,i+r}^{\phantom{\dagger}}}=\, 12[⟨ci,↑†​ci+r,↑​ci+1,↓†​ci+r+1,↓⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\Big[\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\uparrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r,\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{i+1,\downarrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r+1,\downarrow}}
+⟨ci,↑†​ci+r+1,↑​ci+1,↓†​ci+r,↓⟩\displaystyle\hskip 21.68121pt+\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\uparrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r+1,\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{i+1,\downarrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r,\downarrow}}
+⟨ci+1,↑†​ci+r,↑​ci,↓†​ci+r+1,↓⟩\displaystyle\hskip 21.68121pt+\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i+1,\uparrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r,\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{i,\downarrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r+1,\downarrow}}
+⟨ci+1,↑†​ci+r+1,↑​ci,↓†​ci+r,↓⟩],\displaystyle\hskip 21.68121pt+\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i+1,\uparrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r+1,\uparrow}c^{\dagger}_{i,\downarrow}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{i+r,\downarrow}}\Big], (76)

are also measurable in experiments via a combination of experimental techniques, each of which has been demonstrated.

To measure ⟨ci,σ†​cj,σ​ck,τ†​cl,τ⟩\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{k,\tau}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l,\tau}} we can use a method similar to the last subsection, simultaneously rotating on the pair of double wells (i,j)(i,j) and (k,l)(k,l). Using the identity Eq. (73),

⟨ci,σ†​cj,σ​ck,τ†​cl,τ⟩=\displaystyle\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j,\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{k,\tau}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{l,\tau}}=\, 14[⟨X(i,σ)​(j,σ)​X(k,τ)​(l,τ)⟩−⟨Y(i,σ)​(j,σ)​Y(k,τ)​(l,τ)⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{4}\big[\braket{X_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}X_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}}-\braket{Y_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}Y_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}}
+i(⟨X(i,σ)​(j,σ)​Y(k,τ)​(l,τ)⟩+⟨Y(i,σ)​(j,σ)​X(k,τ)​(l,τ)⟩)].\displaystyle+i\left(\braket{X_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}Y_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}}+\braket{Y_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}X_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}}\right)\big]. (77)

From Eqs. (74) and (75), all terms in Eq. (77) can be rotated into diagonal correlators. For example, the first term is

⟨X(i,σ)​(j,σ)​X(k,τ)​(l,τ)⟩=\displaystyle\braket{X_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}X_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}}=\, ⟨Ry(i,σ)​(j,σ)(π/2)Ry(k,τ)​(l,τ)(π/2)Z(i,σ)​(j,σ)Z(k,τ)​(l,τ)Ry(i,σ)​(j,σ)(−π/2)Ry(k,τ)​(l,τ)(−π/2)⟩.\displaystyle\braket{R^{y}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(\pi/2)R^{y}_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}(\pi/2)Z_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}Z_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}R^{y}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(-\pi/2)R^{y}_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}(-\pi/2)}. (78)

The two two-site rotations R(i,σ)​(j,σ)y​(π/2)​R(k,τ)​(l,τ)y​(π/2)R^{y}_{(i,\sigma)(j,\sigma)}(\pi/2)R^{y}_{(k,\tau)(l,\tau)}(\pi/2) can be performed simultaneously. With site-resolved, spin-selective readout via the quantum gas microscope, we can measure Eq. (78) by summing four density-density correlations.

The general four-point correlations ⟨ci,σ†​cj,τ†​ck,η​cl,ξ⟩\braket{c^{\dagger}_{i,\sigma}c^{\dagger}_{j,\tau}c_{k,\eta}^{\phantom{\dagger}}c_{l,\xi}^{\phantom{\dagger}}} can also be measured using the above technique, by first swapping sites using techniques introduced above or additional tweezers. Alternatively, previous studies have also used information scrambling techniques to capture the general four-point correlations [119, 120].

F.3 Girvin-MacDonald correlation

Another type of correlation – the GMD correlation Ci​jGMDC^{\text{GMD}}_{ij}, which can be written as sums of ⟨ai†​nk​nl​…​aj⟩\braket{a^{\dagger}_{i}n_{k}n_{l}\dots a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}} by expanding the exponential in Eq. (12) and using nk2=nkn_{k}^{2}=n_{k} – can also be measured using the double-well rotation on the pair of sites ii and jj and the site-resolved density readout over the lattice. After re-arranging and isolating the double wells (i,j)(i,j) with methods similar to previous cases, the π/2\pi/2 XX and YY rotations transfer the correlation into sums of populations:

⟨ai†​nk​…​aj⟩=\displaystyle\braket{a^{\dagger}_{i}n_{k}\dots a^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}}=\, 12​⟨Xi​j​nk​…⟩+i2​⟨Yi​j​nk​…⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\braket{X_{ij}n_{k}\dots}+\frac{i}{2}\braket{Y_{ij}n_{k}\dots}
=\displaystyle=\, 12​⟨Ryi​j(−π/2)Zi​jRyi​j(π/2)nk…⟩\displaystyle\frac{1}{2}\braket{R^{y}_{ij}(-\pi/2)Z_{ij}R^{y}_{ij}(\pi/2)n_{k}\dots}
−i2​⟨Rxi​j(−π/2)Zi​jRxi​j(π/2)nk…⟩,\displaystyle-\frac{i}{2}\braket{R^{x}_{ij}(-\pi/2)Z_{ij}R^{x}_{ij}(\pi/2)n_{k}\dots}, (79)

where Xi​jX_{ij}, Yi​jY_{ij} and Zi​jZ_{ij} are defined analogously to the fermion bilinears in Eq. (61). The site-resolved density readout in a quantum gas microscope then provides the expectation values ⟨(ni−nj)​nk​nl​…⟩\braket{(n_{i}-n_{j})n_{k}n_{l}\dots}.

In addition to GMD correlations, the above technique allows us to measure density- or spin-conditioned tunneling ci†​nk​cjc^{\dagger}_{i}n^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{k}c^{\phantom{\dagger}}_{j}, extending the range of Hamiltonians that can be simulated.

Appendix G Experiment run-time estimate

This section discusses the number of shots and the total time required for an experiment on quantum hardware to run iterations to reach a 1%1\% VQE algorithm error in our framework. For these proof-of-principle computations, we use the same simple optimization methods described in this text, and we also use only the most naive techniques to estimate the variational energy and its gradient. We expect the optimization cost can be dramatically decreased from these estimates.

We start by considering the experimental time required to measure the energy gradient required by the optimizer, done via naive finite-differences:

∂⟨HT⟩∂θi≈⟨HT​(θi+Δ​θi)⟩−⟨HT​(θi)⟩Δ​θi+O⁡(Δ​θi)\frac{\partial\braket{H_{T}}}{\partial\theta_{i}}\approx\frac{\braket{H_{T}(\theta_{i}+\Delta\theta_{i})}-\braket{H_{T}(\theta_{i})}}{\Delta\theta_{i}}+O(\Delta\theta_{i}) (80)

for small Δ​θi\Delta\theta_{i}. To reach an error in the gradient δ\delta, one needs ∼1/δ2\sim 1/\delta^{2} measurements. We consider a gradient error target Δ​θ=10%\Delta\theta=10\%, requiring ∼102\sim 10^{2} measurements, which leads to an energy error after optimization of ∼1%\sim 1\%. We note that these measurements need not be done serially – in a large system, different regions contribute effectively independent measurements when they are sufficiently separated. A 2D Lm=100L_{m}=100 optical lattice allows one to effectively measure of Lm2/Lc2L^{2}_{m}/L^{2}_{c} independent systems of size LcL_{c} per experiment cycle, where LcL_{c} is a scale large enough that there is little correlation in the measurements.

To obtain the gradient for each optimization iteration, an NlN_{l}-layer, NparamN_{\text{param}}-parameter-per-layer ansatz requires measurements of Nparam​Nl+1N_{\text{param}}N_{l}+1 energy evaluations. For the ansatzes used in this work, this is about 5​Nl5N_{l} evaluations.

The next step is to consider the number of gradients that must be evaluated for the optimizer. We will consider Nl=10N_{l}=10, which typically gives less than 1%1\% variational error. We start by optimizing the Nl=10N_{l}=10 parameters for classically tractable systems, say with L=4L=4 in 2D.

Next, we use the transfer technique by increasing the system size LL by 22. At a target 1%1\% error level, this would usually need 1010 iterations for each LL, as suggested by Fig. C2. (Note that while Fig. C2 used around 10​Nl10N_{l} iterations, this converge the error four orders of magnitude more accurately than required here.) For the finite-size error to be 1%1\%, we need to reach roughly L=20L=20. For each LL, the transfer process needs 5​Nl​Niter≈5005N_{l}N_{\rm iter}\approx 500 energy values. With 10210^{2} measurements needed for each energy value as discussed above, the number of experimental shots for each energy value would be

∑L=4​ step by 220102Lm2/L2≈15.\sum^{20}_{L=4\text{ step by 2}}\frac{10^{2}}{L^{2}_{m}/L^{2}}\approx 15. (81)

Altogether, the total fVQE calculation for variational error, optimization error, and finite-size error each about 1%\% requires about 15×500∼8×10315\times 500\sim 8\times 10^{3} shots. Such shot numbers are routinely employed in papers with quantum gas microscopes [121, 122]. For current fermion experiments, the cycle time is about ∼10​s\sim 10\text{s} [123], so the full calculation takes roughly 2222 hours. We note that the slowest part is the evaporative atom cooling, which might be optimized further or – using tweezer arrays – improved by an order of magnitude or more. A calculation of this accuracy would surpass that achievable for many Hubbard-like problems on classical hardware [97].

The optimization approach used for these estimates leaves substantial room for improvement, possibly by orders of magnitude. More efficient transfer and bootstrapping, more hardware parallelism, faster platforms, and better optimization methods can further reduce the run-time. For example, as alternatives to gradient-based algorithms, we note that gradient-free optimization approaches, such as simplex methods and surrogate model methods, are fully compatible with our framework. The recently proposed fermion-gate-based ansatzes [57, 67] estimate the gradient via the parameter shift method. This reduces the need for high-accuracy quantum measurements, but does not eliminate the essential O⁡(Nparam​Nl)O(N_{\text{param}}N_{l}) gradient measurement overhead. Meanwhile, the variational quantum imaginary-time evolution (VarQITE) method [58] circumvents finite-difference gradient measurements by measuring the quantum geometric tensor ⟨H(m)​H(m′)⟩\braket{H^{(m)}H^{(m^{\prime})}} in each iteration, incurring a severe O⁡(Nparam2​Nl2)O(N^{2}_{\text{param}}N^{2}_{l}) measurement overhead. In general, benchmarking and developing efficient and experiment-friendly optimization methods is an important subject for future study. Nevertheless, the estimates here show that straightforward applications of existing methods plausibly can achieve interesting, difficult to classically simulate, results on existing quantum platforms.

Finally, similar to the discussion of the optimization overhead in App. C, we briefly discuss how measurement repetitions enter the scaling analysis. As discussed in this Appendix, independent measurements used to estimate an observable with statistical error ϵM\epsilon_{M} require O⁡(1/ϵM2)O(1/\epsilon_{M}^{2}) repetitions. Thus the accumulated evolution time for the readout scales as

Ttot∝TϵM2.T_{\rm tot}\propto\frac{T}{\epsilon_{M}^{2}}. (82)

However, like the optimization overhead discussed in App. C, we find that they do not affect the major conclusion of our scaling analysis, as taking ϵM∼ϵ\epsilon_{M}\sim\epsilon only changes the polynomial exponent in 1/ϵ1/\epsilon, and therefore TtotT_{\rm tot} remains O⁡(poly⁡(1/ϵ))O(\mathrm{poly}(1/\epsilon)).

Appendix H Exact ground state of Hofstadter-Hubbard model

This section shows that the ground state of the HHM is a fractional Quantum Hall (FQH) state, with evidence from ED. While extensive studies [43, 73, 74, 75, 69, 72] on the ground state of the fractionally filled 2D HHM have confirmed that its ground state is an FQH state, reproducing the FQH physics for model parameters and system sizes similar to our fVQE results is useful. We consider two aspects: the periodic energy spectrum of the topologically quasi-degenerate ground states when an external flux is inserted adiabatically into 4×64\times 6 and 4×84\times 8 tori, and the existence of edge currents and the vanishing bulk density-density correlations on the open-boundary plane Lx×Ly=5×7L_{x}\times L_{y}=5\times 7 grid.

We first show that the ground state of the Lx=5L_{x}=5 tori with ϕ=2​π/4\phi=2\pi/4 at an appropriate filling is the fractionalized m=2m=2 FQH state. For an FQH system on a torus, the topologically ordered ground-state manifold is expected to exhibit an mm-fold quasi-degeneracy and a nontrivial (integer) Chern number when the entire manifold is treated as a bundle over the two-dimensional space of twisted boundary conditions (θx,θy)(\theta_{x},\theta_{y}). Using the discretized, gauge-invariant Chern-number algorithm by Fukui, Hatsugai and Suzuki [124], we find in both Fig. H1a and Fig. H1b that the mm-fold quasi-degenerate ground-state band carries a total bundle Chern number CFHS=−1C_{\rm FHS}=-1, providing direct evidence for fractionalized topological degeneracy. Moreover, due to the topological nature of the ground state, inserting a flux 2​π2\pi can transfer the system from one ground state to another. The ED computation confirms this behavior for threading a flux with θy\theta_{y} at a system size comparable to that of our fVQE results in the main text. In Fig. H1b, we observe the expected behavior: a 2​m​π2m\pi-periodic pattern in the θy\theta_{y} dependence of the mm-fold quasi-degenerate energy spectrum, while ground states are interchanged after a 2​π2\pi flux insertion, further providing signatures of an FQH state with filling factor mm. A similar flux insertion along xx reveals a more conventional behavior, with a ground state returning to itself after 2​π2\pi flux insertion, presumably due to the shorter length of the system in this direction.

In addition to the torus results, the ED ground state on a 5×75\times 7 lattice with open boundary conditions also exhibits signatures of the FQH state. We calculate currents and density-density correlations for lattices with various fluxes per plaquette ϕ/(2​π)=1/8\phi/(2\pi)=1/8, 1/41/4, and 3/83/8, with particle number Np=2N_{p}=2, 33, and 44 appropriate for the m=2m=2 FQH state by the formula Np=ϕ​N□/(2​π​m)N_{p}=\phi N_{\Box}/(2\pi m) where N□=(Lx−1)×(Ly−1)N_{\Box}=(L_{x}-1)\times(L_{y}-1) is the number of plaquettes. Fig. H2 shows that the bulk cyclotron currents are suppressed as NpN_{p} is increased, while chiral edge currents develop. The bulk density-density correlations (as defined in Eq. (11)) near the lattice center 𝒓=𝟎\bm{r}=\bm{0} vanish at ϕ/(2​π)=1/4\phi/(2\pi)=1/4 filling, indicating the anti-correlation typical of a Laughlin state. These results further show that the ground state of the HHM at a flux per plaquette ϕ/(2​π)=1/4\phi/(2\pi)=1/4 with appropriate particle filling indeed exhibits features characteristic of the FQH state.
